newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU probes Italian cheese scare.
newsitem.headline: EU probes Italian cheese scare.

text.p: The European Commission is investigating a botulism scare in Italy linked to the death of a teenage boy who had eaten mascarpone cheese, a European Commission spokesman said on Tuesday.

Italian health inspectors said on Monday they had pulled some 100,000 tubs of mascarpone -- a soft, sweet cheese -- from stores after the boy died in Naples on Saturday after eating home-made tiramisu, a sponge dessert prepared with the cheese.

"A Commission official went to Italy to investigate," Commission spokesman Jean-Christophe Filori told a briefing, adding that the official will return at the end of the week to report whether all necessary measures had been implemented.
If not, EU safeguard action may be taken, Filori said.

Under the EU rapid alert system, the Commission immediately informed countries to which the cheese was exported -- Belgium, Spain, Sweden and Austria -- after being informed by the Italian authorities, he said.

Belgium said on Monday it would withdraw all mascarpone sold under the Giglio, Parmalat and Sol di Valle brand names, while Sweden warned consumers not to eat those brands until more was known about the scare.
At least seven certified cases of botulism have arisen in the Naples area, the Calabria region on the toe of Italy and the central town of Siena.
All have been linked to a batch of mascarpone with a sell-by date of October 3 produced by one manufacturer in the northern town of Reggio Emilia.
Botulism is a severe form of poisoning from foods that contain a toxin which can affect the central nervous system. In fatal cases, death is often caused by heart and lung failure.
The bacterium is most typically found in improperly preserved canned raw meat.
